summary: Per-file resilience audit → fair-budget adversarial verification gate → grounded synthesis
logs: gate: 5 passed, 1 refuted, 7 held, 24 side leads

rootCauses.title: Blocking Await.result on shared default ExecutionContext in placeOrder
rootCauses.rationale: Line 12 calls Await.result on payments.charge for up to 30s inside a Future on the default injected ExecutionContext, with no blocking{} wrapper and no dedicated executor, so it ties up a shared pool thread for that whole time.

rootCauses.title: Unbounded cached thread pool for inventory message processing
rootCauses.rationale: The workers pool uses Executors.newCachedThreadPool(), which has no upper limit on threads, and onMessage submits one task per message, so a burst of messages or a slow stock service can create threads without limit.

rootCauses.title: Non-idempotent payment charge retried without Idempotency-Key
rootCauses.rationale: POST /charges is retried on any failure with no Idempotency-Key header, so a call that timed out or failed after the server processed it can charge the customer twice.

rootCauses.title: ShippingGateway RestTemplate has no connect/read timeout
rootCauses.rationale: The RestTemplate is built with its no-arg constructor, so it uses SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory with no connect or read timeout (0 means infinite), and nothing else sets one.

rootCauses.title: placeOrder swallows all exceptions into None without logging
rootCauses.rationale: The .recover { case _: Exception => None } catches every Exception from the insert, the payment charge, the timeout and the JSON parse and turns it into None; nothing logs or rethrows it, so the caller cannot tell what failed.

notInEvidence: Whether the retry in chargeWithRetry has any attempt cap or backoff (code shown does not show a bound check)
Whether Thread.sleep(200) in placeOrder also blocks the shared pool materially (not stated as a defect)
Whether F4's infinite timeout can exhaust a shared request thread pool (system-level impact not established)
Whether F5 hides a successful charge followed by a failed parse, causing order/payment inconsistency
Whether repo.insert in placeOrder is a blocking JDBC call

findings.defect: The non-idempotent POST /charges is retried on any failure with no Idempotency-Key header, so a call that timed out or failed after the server processed it can charge the customer twice.

The workers pool is built with Executors.newCachedThreadPool(), which has no upper limit on threads, and onMessage submits one task per message, so a burst of messages or a slow stock service can create threads without limit.

findings.verifiedCode: private final RestTemplate rest = new RestTemplate();
findings.defect: The RestTemplate on line 12 is built with its no-arg constructor, so it uses SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory with no connect or read timeout (0 means infinite), and nothing else sets one.

The `.recover { case _: Exception => None }` on line 15 catches every Exception from the insert, the payment charge, the timeout and the JSON parse, and turns it into None. Nothing logs it and nothing rethrows it, so the caller cannot tell what failed.

rejected.why: Line 18 is not a blocking-in-async defect: the blocking repo call is wrapped in `blocking {}` and runs on a dedicated `blockingEc` executor, not the default async pool.

leads.observation: Line 13: Thread.sleep(200) also blocks the default pool thread.
Line 11: repo.insert is a synchronous call, likely blocking DB I/O, and it also runs on the default ec.

Line 15: recover { case _: Exception => None } swallows every failure, including a payment timeout that happens after the order is inserted. This can leave an order persisted but not charged, and nothing makes it visible.
repo.insert happens before the charge, and nothing compensates or uses an idempotency key if the charge fails.
The retry has no limit: attempt goes up but is never checked, so a failing request retries forever.
There is no backoff between retries.
recoverWith uses `case _`, so it retries every error, including 4xx-style failures that will never succeed.
The charge POST has no request timeout, while refundStatus sets one of 3 seconds.
In refundStatus, `.recover { ... throw e }` only logs and rethrows. That is harmless, but `recover` is not needed for it.
Line 13: the LinkedBlockingQueue inbox has no capacity limit, so it can also grow without bound.
Lines 33-34: the empty catch block swallows exceptions, so a failed reserve call is lost with no retry and no log entry.
There is no shutdown of the executor (no @PreDestroy).
The reserve POST has no idempotency key.
@Retryable(maxAttempts = 10) on createShipment retries a non-idempotent POST without an idempotency key, so a retry can create duplicate shipments. It also sets no backoff and no retry filter.
trackingStatus runs supplyAsync on the shared ForkJoinPool common pool instead of a dedicated executor, and it does not cancel the future after a timeout, so blocked threads can pile up.
trackingStatus declares throws Exception and lets TimeoutException and ExecutionException through without wrapping them.
Line 12: Await.result blocks for up to 30s on the default ExecutionContext. The call is not wrapped in blocking{} and does not use blockingEc.
Line 13: Thread.sleep(200) blocks a thread of the default ExecutionContext.
Line 11: repo.insert is a synchronous DB call on the default EC. It runs before the charge and is not compensated, so a failed charge leaves an orphan order.
There is no idempotency key on payments.charge. The order.id is passed, but whether it is used as an idempotency key is unknown.
Line 12: Await.result(payments.charge(...), 30.seconds) inside a Future on the default ec is a real blocking-in-async defect.
Line 13: Thread.sleep(200) on the default ec also blocks it.
Line 11: repo.insert runs on the default ec with no blocking wrapper.
Line 15: recover turns every Exception into None, which hides failures; the charge may also be retried without an idempotency key.
